tldr: By providing pre-rendered "future body appearance" derived from robot kinematics as an input, the video world model Doppel focuses on predicting physical dynamics, predicting motions across eight different robot and human embodiments within a single model.
hero_caption: Concept diagram of the proposed method, Doppel. Across single robot arms, human upper bodies, and multi-DoF humanoids, future body appearances are rendered along commanded trajectories as conditioning. This allows a single shared model to accurately predict environmental responses while significantly reducing required training samples.
overview:
Action-conditioned video world models are a promising approach for simulating how the surrounding environment changes as a result of robot actions. However, most conventional models only took numerical joint action vectors as input. They had to learn two difficult problems from scratch simultaneously: how the robot itself moves from the camera's perspective given those actions, and how the environment responds when the robot touches an object. Although the robot's arm shape and joint kinematics are already known from design blueprints (URDF), existing approaches failed to leverage this geometric information at all.

To address this, the authors came up with a natural idea: simply pre-render the robot's intended future motion and show it to the model. Using forward kinematics and a differentiable renderer along a planned joint trajectory, camera-aligned 3D Gaussian renderings of the robot are generated and fed into the video model. This frees the model from dedicating capacity to predicting its own body pose. Instead, it can focus entirely on modeling environmental responses, such as how contacted objects tilt, slide, or lift. Furthermore, unifying robot motion into an image-space rendering provides a common interface across different robots and human bodies with varying numbers of joints and control spaces, allowing them to be trained together under a single set of network weights.

The authors implemented this approach in a model called Doppel. It was trained on eight embodiments totaling around 600 hours of video: three robot arms (Franka, UR5e, and WidowX), a bimanual arm, an egocentric humanoid with dexterous hands, and three human hand/body datasets. As a result, prediction accuracy on unseen objects and environments improved substantially, achieving high-accuracy predictions with roughly 60% fewer training samples compared to conventional action-only methods.
contributions: Proposed an embodiment-agnostic conditioning method that combines numerical action trajectories with camera-aligned robot renderings generated via forward kinematics and differentiable rendering, absorbing structural differences across bodies into a shared image space.

Successfully co-trained a single shared network across eight diverse embodiments—including three single arms, a bimanual arm, a humanoid robot, and human hands and full bodies—without providing any embodiment identity labels.

Introduced an evaluation framework that separates the robot region from the moving object (manipulation target) region in addition to full-frame image quality, demonstrating clear improvements in the consistency of contact-driven object dynamics over baselines.
Established and released a calibration pipeline that automatically recovers high-precision camera poses from offline datasets lacking camera extrinsics using a differentiable renderer.

sections.heading: If We Already Know the Robot's Body, Why Not Just Render It?
sections.summary: Just as humans know where their arms are and focus on how a cup moves, robots should leverage known geometry. This section explains the motivation and concept behind Doppel: rendering the robot's future motion in image space to let the video model focus its capacity on environmental dynamics.
sections.details:
When we reach out to grasp a cup, visual and proprioceptive feedback already tell us roughly where our arm will move. The real uncertainty that requires prediction is the external response: whether the cup will slip, tip over, or be grasped securely. Conventional video world models in robotics were conditioned purely on numerical vectors such as joint angles. As a result, they tried to learn both the geometric projection of the robot's motion and the physics of environmental interaction within a single black-box model.

However, a robot's link lengths and range of motion (kinematics) are perfectly known from its URDF file. The key insight is that if we pre-render this known body motion as camera-aligned computer graphics and feed it into the video model, the model is relieved of an unnecessary burden. It can dedicate all its capacity to predicting contacts and object movements. Based on this idea, the authors introduced Doppel, named after the German word for "lookalike" or "double."

This approach also offers a major advantage: it acts as a common language for handling robots with different physical structures within a single model. Robot arms like Franka (7-DoF), UR5e (6-DoF), and WidowX have different joint counts and control commands. When viewed as rendered body motion in an image, however, they share the exact same pixel space. This allows manipulation data from multiple robots and humans to be fed into a single foundation video generation model for joint training.

sections.heading: Where Video Generation Meets Robotics Geometry: How It Differs from Past World Models
sections.summary: This section reviews the trend of using video prediction models as robot simulators and compares prior geometric conditioning and multi-embodiment learning techniques. Unlike methods that only provide joint skeletons or end-effector positions, Doppel fully captures 3D link geometry and self-occlusion.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Video World Models
With the rapid rise of video diffusion and flow matching models, repurposing them as action simulators for robotics has attracted significant interest. However, most models inject numerical action vectors directly into frame tokens or temporal embeddings. They rely on brute-force training over massive datasets to align actions with arm movements on screen.

Attempts to incorporate explicit geometric information include projecting joint skeletons, feeding end-effector position maps, or utilizing 3D point clouds and occupancy grids. However, skeletons and end-effector coordinates fail to represent arm thickness, gripper details, and self-occlusions (where the arm hides the workspace). Doppel is unique because it renders the complete, multi-joint 3D body directly into camera view using 3D Gaussian Splatting, a technique that represents and renders 3D shapes quickly via collections of Gaussians.

### Challenges in Multi-Embodiment Learning
When training a single policy on data from different robots, past approaches often required separate embodiment-specific action heads or segmentation masks to erase the robot from the image. Doppel uses a differentiable renderer to convert any robot's motion into a standardized camera-aligned rendering. Consequently, the same encoder and video backbone can directly learn behaviors across diverse embodiments without requiring embodiment-specific output heads.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Latent Video Flow Matching and Differentiable Rendering
sections.summary: This section explains the formulation of the Latent Flow Matching Transformer used for video generation and the 3D Gaussian rendering framework that synthesizes camera-aligned images from robot URDFs in real time.
sections.details:
The goal is to learn a single visual forward dynamics model $\theta$ that predicts future observation frames given an initial frame $\mathbf{o}_0$ and a planned joint configuration trajectory $a^e_{1:T-1}$. Although the joint space dimension $d_e$ and geometry vary for each embodiment $e$, the model parameters $\theta$ are completely shared.

### Latent Video Flow Matching
The base video generator is a pretrained Rectified Flow image-to-video model (Wan 2.1). Video frame sequences are compressed into a latent space representation $\mathbf{z}$ by a pretrained temporally causal VAE. The model linearly interpolates between noise $\bm{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and the original latents $\mathbf{z}$ across flow matching timesteps $\tau \in [0, 1]$, learning to predict the target velocity vector $\bm{\epsilon} - \mathbf{z}$. The initial frame is replaced with clean latent features and kept fixed, computing loss only over future frames.

### Differentiable Robot Rendering
To render each robot's geometry, the authors use the "Dr. Robot" framework. The robot in its rest pose is represented as a set of 3D Gaussians $\mathcal{G}^0_e$. Forward kinematics (FK) computes transformation matrices for each link from joint configurations $a^e_t$. Each Gaussian is transformed and color-adjusted via linear blend skinning $D_e$ and a pose-dependent appearance model $X_e$. It is then rendered using a differentiable rasterizer with camera intrinsics $K_i$ and extrinsics $C_i$. This produces a robot-only image sequence $r^e_{0:T-1}$ perfectly aligned with the camera viewpoint.

captions.F2: Overview of the Doppel architecture. Inputs consist of the initial observation image, the future robot rendering sequence from the differentiable renderer, and numerical action trajectories. These condition the video backbone via token-wise timestep modulation.

sections.heading: Inside Doppel: Auto-Estimating Missing Camera Poses and Blending Renderings with Actions
sections.summary: This section details the preprocessing pipeline that recovers missing camera extrinsics using a differentiable renderer and DINOv2 features, as well as the cross-attention architecture that merges rendered images and numerical vectors to modulate the Transformer.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Automatic Recovery of Camera Extrinsics
Accurately overlaying robot renderings onto real video requires the camera's 6-DoF pose relative to the robot base (camera extrinsics). However, many publicly available open datasets lack calibration data or contain inaccuracies.

To solve this, the authors built an analysis-by-synthesis pipeline that automatically estimates camera extrinsics using gradients from the differentiable renderer. The camera pose is optimized by minimizing an alignment loss combining RGB pixel error, optical flow (estimated via RAFT), and DINOv2 feature similarity between real footage and rendered images. By running parallel optimizations from multiple coarse search initializations, they reliably recover accurate extrinsics even from in-the-wild datasets without checkerboard markers.

### 4.2 Dense Fusion of Renderings and Numerical Actions
Once future robot renderings are generated, they are injected into the video generation model. The rendering sequence is mapped to the latent space using the same frozen VAE as the main video. After mean-subtraction normalization, a small 3D convolutional encoder and self-attention transform it into spatial-temporal tokens.

Meanwhile, numerical action vectors (joint angles and gripper states) are zero-padded to a shared 159-dimensional vector across embodiments, followed by a shared MLP and temporal embeddings. The critical step is a cross-attention layer where rendering tokens act as Queries, and numerical action tokens act as Keys and Values. This integrates "where the arm is on screen and what its joint states are" into a single dense conditioning vector $g_j$. Joint information along the depth axis and gripper pinch forces—which might be visually occluded—are complemented by the numerical tokens.

The resulting conditioning vector $g_j$ is added token-wise to the timestep embeddings inside the Transformer blocks, directly modulating the Attention and Feed-Forward layers throughout the network. No embodiment identification tokens (embodiment IDs) are used; the visual appearance of the rendering itself indicates the body type to the model.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: Stress-Testing Across Three Arms, Full-Body Humanoids, and Humans
sections.summary: This section covers the data configuration of "Doppel-3" (using Franka, UR5e, and WidowX) and "Doppel-8" (adding humanoids and human datasets), along with rigorous evaluation metrics that decouple objects from the robot.
sections.details:
### Datasets and Embodiment Variations
For foundational experiments, the authors built "Doppel-3" by aggregating three widely used robotics datasets:
- DROID: Franka Emika Panda (7-DoF) + 2-finger gripper
- RoboMIND: UR5e (6-DoF) + 2-finger gripper
- Bridge: WidowX (6-DoF)

To test the limits of generalization, they expanded this to "Doppel-8," covering eight distinct embodiments. The additions include the bimanual YAM robot (ABC dataset), the Vega-1 humanoid robot with dexterous hands (T-Rex dataset), and three human motion datasets with fitted 3D meshes for hands, upper bodies, and full bodies (GigaHands, OakInk2, Ego-Exo4D). Across roughly 600 hours of multi-embodiment video, the single shared model was trained without any embodiment labels.

### Evaluation Protocol and Disentangled Metrics
To properly evaluate generalization, test splits were prepared not only for unseen trajectories in familiar environments (Validation) but also for out-of-distribution (OOD) settings involving completely unseen labs, novel kitchens, and unfamiliar objects.

Evaluation metrics include full-frame PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, as well as the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), which tracks object masks using SAM2. Crucially, the authors evaluate these metrics separately across the full frame, the robot region, and the moving object (manipulation target) region. This distinguishes whether the robot rendering simply matches the view or whether the manipulated object actually moves correctly.

Baselines include an Action-only model (following the EgoWM format) and OSCAR, a state-of-the-art method conditioned on projected joint skeletons.

sections.heading: Results: Physical Failures Plummet and Training Efficiency Surges by Over 60%
sections.summary: Doppel improved PSNR by up to 1.5 dB over baselines, drastically improving consistency during object lifting and contact interactions. Remarkably, co-training on eight embodiments further boosted prediction performance on single robots.
sections.details:
### Dramatic Gains in Prediction Accuracy
Across the three robot arm datasets, Doppel achieved clear visual quality improvements over action-only and skeleton-based (OSCAR) models on all evaluation splits. It achieved an average PSNR improvement of 1.00 dB on unseen trajectories and 1.20 dB in challenging OOD environments with novel rooms and objects.

Region-specific analysis revealed even more compelling results. In the Action-only baseline, physical failures occurred frequently: the arm moved to the target position, but vegetables or cups on the table remained frozen in place (the robot passed right through them). In contrast, Doppel dramatically improved object PSNR (jumping from 21.50 dB to 24.85 dB on Bridge OOD) and object SCS (rising from 0.778 to 0.831). The dynamics of objects lifting and rotating upon contact were captured accurately.

### Heterogeneous Embodiments Help Robot Predictions
The most surprising finding came from "Doppel-8." Adding humanoid and human hand videos improved robot arm prediction accuracy (PSNR and SSIM on DROID and RoboMIND) beyond Doppel-3, even though no additional Franka or UR5e data was added. Doppel-8 outperformed Doppel-3 on four out of six robot evaluation splits. As long as body renderings provide a common format, basic physical laws of contact and manipulation transfer effectively across humans and robots.

### Sample Efficiency and Long-Horizon Rollouts
In terms of training efficiency, Doppel matched or exceeded the PSNR and SCS of the shared Action-only baseline using only 36.2% of the training steps (requiring 63.8% fewer data samples). Injecting known geometric information sped up convergence significantly. Furthermore, using autoregressive rollouts—feeding predicted frames back into the model—Doppel generated coherent interaction videos over a long horizon of 25.6 seconds starting from just a single initial frame.

From left to right: initial frame, input robot rendering sequence, and generated future video. The model predicts natural grasping and contact actions without collapse, even in novel scenes.

sections.heading: Looking Ahead: Body Geometry as the Bridge for General World Models
sections.summary: This section summarizes the benefits of rendering known kinematics to guide world models, while discussing current limitations such as reliance on camera extrinsics and potential zero-shot adaptation to unseen embodiments.
sections.details:
Doppel separates robot body motion from external environmental reactions. By explicitly feeding the former to the model as geometric renderings, the world model can concentrate on learning the true physics of the scene. This architectural paradigm paves the way for a single, unified world model that scales across diverse robots and human actions.

However, several challenges remain for broader deployment. The primary constraint is the prerequisite of accurate robot URDFs (3D models) and camera extrinsics relative to the base. While camera extrinsics were recovered via offline optimization in this work, handling dynamic camera setups—such as handheld or rapidly moving viewpoints—remains open for future research. In addition, the current model evaluates embodiments seen during training; extending this to zero-shot physical prediction on entirely unseen robot URDFs and multi-view camera setups presents an exciting future direction.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind the Scenes of 3D Gaussian Rendering and Camera Alignment
sections.summary: This section provides supplementary details on the rendering pipeline from 3D meshes for robots and humans, highlighting the precise calibration alignment between real RGB video and synthetic renderings.
sections.details:
In the rendering pipeline using the differentiable renderer "Dr. Robot," 3D Gaussians corresponding to each robot link are learned in advance, then deformed and rendered in real time based on commanded joint angles. Sampling indices for real RGB frames and rendered frames are matched exactly to eliminate temporal misalignment.

Similar care was taken for additional embodiments. A Dr. Robot model was constructed for the bimanual YAM arm, while the Vega-1 humanoid was rasterized directly from its official URDF mesh. For human datasets, fitted 3D meshes from MANO (hands), SMPL-X (upper body), and SMPL-H (full body) were rendered on a black background using dataset-specific camera models including distortion correction. Across all datasets, the rendered bodies align closely with the real video footage at the pixel level.

captions.F10: Comparison between real RGB images (top row) and robot renderings based on auto-recovered camera extrinsics (bottom row) across DROID, Bridge, and RoboMIND. Complex arm poses and gripper angles align closely with the real footage.

takeaways: Injecting inductive bias by rendering known forward kinematics and geometry—rather than forcing neural networks to learn them from scratch—boosts training efficiency by over 60% and dramatically improves physical prediction accuracy.

Unifying robot movements into an on-screen rendered representation removes boundaries between differing joint spaces, enabling scaled co-training of multiple robots and humans on a shared video foundation model.
Co-training on human and heterogeneous robot data transfers interaction dynamics across embodiments, improving physical prediction accuracy even for specific single-arm setups.
limitations: Requires an accurate URDF (3D geometric model) of the robot and calibrated camera extrinsics beforehand.
Does not support dynamic camera environments where viewpoints move substantially during execution or where extrinsics change on the fly.
Zero-shot adaptation to completely novel robot embodiments (unseen URDFs) not present during training has not yet been demonstrated.
